\\mathbf{\\omega}.name: Angular Velocity Vector
\\mathbf{\\omega}.description: A vector quantity that describes the rate of rotation and the axis of rotation of an object. Its direction is along the axis of rotation, and its magnitude is the angular speed.

\\mathbf{L}.name: Angular Momentum Vector
\\mathbf{L}.description: A vector quantity representing the 'quantity of motion' in rotation. For a rigid body, it is defined as the product of the inertia tensor and the angular velocity vector. Its direction is typically along the axis of rotation, but can change if external torques are applied.

alignment-rule-a56ed43a.interpretation: In this equation, $\mathbf{\omega}$ represents the angular velocity vector, which describes the rate and axis of rotation of a rigid body. Its SI units are radians per second (rad/s). $\mathbf{L}$ represents the angular momentum vector, a measure of the rotational inertia of a body about an axis. Its SI units are kilogram meter squared per second (kg $m^2$/s). The equation $\mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{L}$ eq 0$signifies that the vector \mathbf{\omega} is not parallel or anti-parallel to the vector \mathbf{L} . The cross product \mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{L} results in a vector that is perpendicular to both \mathbf{\omega} and \mathbf{L} , and its magnitude is given by$|$\mathbf{\omega}$| |$\mathbf{L}$| $\sin$( $\theta$)$, where \theta is the angle between \mathbf{\omega} and \mathbf{L} . For the cross product to be non-zero, \sin$( $\theta$)$must be non-zero, meaning \theta cannot be 0 or \pi radians. Physically, a non-zero \mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{L} implies the presence of an external torque \boldsymbol{\tau} acting on the system, according to the rotational analogue of Newton's second law: \boldsymbol{\tau} = \frac{d \mathbf{L}$}{dt}$. When \mathbf{ \omega } \times \mathbf{L}$ eq 0$, the angular momentum \mathbf{L} is not constant in time, which means there must be a net torque applied to the body. This situation often arises in the context of gyroscopic precession, where the axis of rotation itself changes direction$.
alignment-rule-a56ed43a.symmetry_origin: This condition arises from the relationship between angular velocity, angular momentum, and torque in classical mechanics. Specifically, it relates to the breakdown of axial symmetry when the angular velocity vector is not aligned with a principal axis of inertia, or when external torques are applied. The equation is a direct consequence of the definition of angular momentum for a rigid body, $\mathbf{L} = \boldsymbol{I} \boldsymbol{\omega}$, where $\boldsymbol{I}$ is the inertia tensor. If $\boldsymbol{I}$ is not aligned with $\mathbf{\omega} (i.e., \boldsymbol{I} is not a scalar multiple of the identity tensor when expressed in the rotating frame aligned with \mathbf{\omega} ), then \mathbf{L}$ will not be parallel to $\mathbf{\omega}$, leading to $\mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{L} eq 0$.
alignment-rule-a56ed43a.limits_and_boundary: As the angle $\theta$ between $\mathbf{\omega}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ approaches 0 or $\pi$ radians (i.e., the vectors become parallel or anti-parallel), the magnitude of the cross product $|\mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{L}|$ approaches 0. This occurs when the angular velocity vector is aligned with a principal axis of inertia and there are no external torques. Conversely, as the angle $\theta$ approaches $\pi/2$ radians (i.e., the vectors are perpendicular), the magnitude of the cross product reaches its maximum, $|\mathbf{\omega}| |\mathbf{L}|$. If either $|\mathbf{\omega}| \to 0$ or $|\mathbf{L}| \to 0$, the cross product also approaches 0, indicating no rotation or no angular momentum, respectively, and thus no torque associated with their misalignment.
alignment-rule-a56ed43a.conceptual_definition: The formula $\mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{L}$ eq 0$describes a fundamental condition in rotational dynamics. It states that if a system is rotating with an angular velocity \mathbf{\omega} and possesses an angular momentum \mathbf{L} , and the cross product of these two vectors is non-zero, it implies a specific relationship between their orientations and magnitudes. This non-zero cross product is often associated with systems where the principal axes of inertia are not aligned with the axis of rotation, leading to precession or torque$.
alignment-rule-a56ed43a.intuitive_summary: A rotating object experiences a torque if its angular velocity is not aligned with its angular momentum.

The quantity $N_{\text{stars}}$ represents the discrete count of stars included in the sample. As $N_{\text{stars}} \to \infty$, the random errors cancel incoherently, leading to precision improvements determined solely by the sample volume.

statistical-gain-24f49b37.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $N_{\text{stars}} \to \infty$, the random statistical error $\sigma_d \to 0$, revealing the true underlying parameter unless bounded by systematic instrumental ceilings. In the limit $N_{\text{stars}} = 1$, the uncertainty is simply the intrinsic single-measurement dispersion $\sigma_d = \sigma_0$.
statistical-gain-24f49b37.conceptual_definition: The statistical gain formula $\sigma_d \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\text{stars}}}}$ expresses the standard error of an averaged astrophysical observable $\sigma_d$ (such as velocity dispersion, mean distance modulus, or metallicity) as a function of the number of independently sampled tracer stars $N_{\text{stars}}$. statistical-gain-24f49b37.description: Quantifies the suppression of statistical uncertainty or dispersion in estimated astrophysical quantities, scaling inversely with the square root of the stellar sample size according to the central limit theorem.

energy-bound-007d7688.symmetry_origin: Lorentz invariance (invariance under $SO(1,3)$ Lorentz transformations) and spacetime translation invariance via Noether's theorem, ensuring the conservation of the four-momentum $P^\mu$.
energy-bound-007d7688.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit ($|\mathbf{p}| \ll mc$), Taylor expanding $E = mc^2 \sqrt{1 + \mathbf{p}^2/(m^2 c^2)}$ yields $E \approx mc^2 + \frac{\mathbf{p}^2}{2m}$, recovering Newtonian kinetic energy plus rest mass. energy-bound-007d7688.intuitive_summary: Total energy consists of two orthogonal components in spacetime: kinetic energy derived from spatial motion through momentum, and intrinsic rest-mass energy derived from the particle's movement through time.

The parameters $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ represent the magnetic permeabilities of the first and second media, respectively. When a field line transitions into a material with significantly higher permeability ($\mu_2 \gg \mu_1$), the refracted angle satisfies $\tan \theta_2 = (\mu_2 / \mu_1) \tan \theta_1 \gg 1$, bending the field line parallel to the surface inside medium 2, or conversely causing external lines to meet a high-$\mu$ medium nearly perpendicular to the boundary.
flux-control-67ee8cfd.symmetry_origin: Translational and rotational invariance in the plane of the interface combined with U(1) gauge invariance of the vector potential $\mathbf{A}$, enforcing normal continuity of $\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}$.
flux-control-67ee8cfd.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of a high-permeability ferromagnetic medium or ideal magnetic conductor ($\mu_2 \to \infty$), field lines in medium 1 meet the interface normally ($\theta_1 \to 0$ for any non-parallel internal angle $\theta_2 < \pi/2$). For identical media ($\mu_1 = \mu_2$), the boundary is transparent ($\theta_1 = \theta_2$). If a non-zero free surface current $\mathbf{K}_f \neq 0$ is present, the tangential boundary condition acquires a discontinuity and the standard tangent ratio is modified.
flux-control-67ee8cfd.conceptual_definition: The tangent law for the refraction of magnetic field lines is derived from standard electromagnetic interface boundary conditions: the continuity of the normal component of magnetic flux density ($B_{1\perp} = B_{2\perp}$) originating from Gauss's law for magnetism ($\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0$), and the continuity of the tangential component of magnetic field intensity ($H_{1\parallel} = H_{2\parallel}$) from Ampère's law ($\nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}_f$) with zero free surface current density ($\mathbf{K}_f = 0$). flux-control-67ee8cfd.intuitive_summary: Just as light rays refract at optical boundaries, magnetic flux lines bend when transitioning between materials of differing permeability. Highly permeable materials effectively 'pull' flux lines toward their surface, making field lines in high-permeability media enter or exit nearly perpendicular to the boundary.
flux-control-67ee8cfd.description: Governs the angular deflection of magnetic field lines across the interface between two linear, isotropic magnetic media with permeabilities $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ in the absence of free surface currents.

The vector $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ is the constant angular velocity vector of the non-inertial coordinate system relative to an inertial background, and $\mathbf{r}$ denotes the position vector relative to the chosen origin on the rotation axis. The term $(\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r})$ represents the instantaneous tangential velocity of the coordinate frame at position $\mathbf{r}$. The negative sign and factor of $1/2$ ensure that the resulting acceleration field $\mathbf{a}_{\text{cf}} = -\nabla \Phi_{\text{fict}} = \omega^2 \mathbf{r}_\perp$ points radially outward from the axis of rotation.
equivalence-link-82f453b2.symmetry_origin: Rooted in the spatial coordinate transformation between inertial and uniformly rotating Euclidean frames under the Galilean group, reflecting the rotational gauge freedom of the Lagrangian formulation in rotating coordinates.
equivalence-link-82f453b2.limits_and_boundary: As $|\boldsymbol{\omega}| \to 0$, the frame becomes inertial and $\Phi_{\text{fict}} \to 0$. equivalence-link-82f453b2.conceptual_definition: In a non-inertial reference frame rotating with uniform angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}$, the position-dependent centrifugal pseudo-force field $\mathbf{g}_{\text{cf}} = -\boldsymbol{\omega} \times (\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r})$ is conservative ($\nabla \times \mathbf{g}_{\text{cf}} = 0$). equivalence-link-82f453b2.intuitive_summary: The centrifugal potential functions like an inverted parabolic landscape that slopes steeply downward as one moves away from the axis of rotation, capturing the outward centrifugal push purely as a gradient descent.
equivalence-link-82f453b2.description: Defines the specific centrifugal potential energy field per unit mass arising in a uniformly rotating coordinate frame. The gradient of this scalar potential yields the fictitious centrifugal acceleration experienced by co-rotating bodies.

the-coriolis-shift-703aaf6f.symmetry_origin: Originates from the non-invariance of the Galilean time derivative operator under time-dependent $SO(3)$ rotational gauge transformations of spatial coordinate frames: $\left(\frac{d}{dt}\right)_{\text{inertial}} = \left(\frac{d}{dt}\right)_{\text{rot}} + \boldsymbol{\omega} \times$.

the-coriolis-shift-703aaf6f.conceptual_definition: The Coriolis acceleration $\mathbf{a}_{\text{cor}} = 2\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{v}$ arises from the cross-term in the second time derivative of the position vector when transforming from an inertial frame to a rotating reference frame. the-coriolis-shift-703aaf6f.intuitive_summary: As an object moves across a rotating platform, the local linear speed of the floor beneath it continuously changes, and its velocity vector rotates relative to the external space, producing a net sideways pseudo-acceleration with a prefactor of two.
the-coriolis-shift-703aaf6f.description: Quantifies the apparent kinematic acceleration experienced by a body moving with relative velocity in a uniformly rotating reference frame.

technical-relation-7a8806e6.interpretation: The field $V(r, \theta)$ denotes the electrostatic or gravitational potential at radial distance $r$ and polar angle $\theta$. The series sums over all angular momentum modes $l \in \mathbb{N}_0$. The angular dependence is weighted by the Legendre polynomials $P_l(\cos\theta)$, and the expansion coefficients $A_l$ and $B_l$ are determined uniquely by Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions.
technical-relation-7a8806e6.symmetry_origin: $SO(3)$ rotational invariance broken down to continuous $SO(2) \cong U(1)$ axial symmetry about the $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$-axis, which restricts the general spherical harmonics $Y_l^m(\theta, \phi)$ to the $m = 0$ subspace.
technical-relation-7a8806e6.limits_and_boundary: As $r \to \infty$, boundary regularity for isolated source systems requires $A_l = 0$ for all $l > 0$, ensuring $V(r, \theta) \to 0$. As $r \to 0$, regularity at the origin for source-free interior regions requires $B_l = 0$ for all $l \ge 0$ to avoid unphysical singularities. For $l = 0$, the $B_0 / r$ term recovers the isotropic Coulomb or Newtonian monopole potential.
technical-relation-7a8806e6.conceptual_definition: The general solution to the Laplace equation $\nabla^2 V(r, \theta) = 0$ in three-dimensional spherical coordinates under azimuthal symmetry ($\partial V / \partial \phi = 0$) is obtained via the separation of variables $V(r, \theta) = R(r) \Theta(\theta)$. The angular solutions regular on the interval $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ are the Legendre polynomials $P_l(\cos\theta)$, while the radial solutions satisfy Euler-Cauchy equations yielding $r^l$ (interior modes) and $r^{-(l+1)}$ (exterior modes).
technical-relation-7a8806e6.intuitive_summary: Any static potential with rotational symmetry around the z-axis in empty space can be decomposed into an infinite sum of multipole moments, where each degree $l$ represents a specific geometric configuration (monopole, dipole, quadrupole, etc.) balancing growing and decaying radial fields.
technical-relation-7a8806e6.description: Expresses the general scalar electrostatic or gravitational potential in a charge-free, azimuthally symmetric region as a multipole series expansion over radial powers and Legendre polynomials.

\\mathrm{Tr}.name: Trace Operator
\\mathrm{Tr}.description: Sum of diagonal elements over an orthonormal basis of the Hilbert space

shared-information-384ac575.interpretation: The quantity $S(\rho)$ denotes the von Neumann entropy. The density operator $\rho = |\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ represents a pure state in Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. The matrix logarithm $\ln \rho$ and trace functional $\mathrm{Tr}$ compute the expectation value of the information content operator. The condition $S(\rho) = 0$ is both necessary and sufficient for a quantum state to be pure, contrasting with mixed states where $S(\rho) > 0$. In bipartite entangled systems, the global state may have $S(\rho_{AB}) = 0$ while reduced subsystem states exhibit entanglement entropy $S(\rho_A) = S(\rho_B) > 0$.
shared-information-384ac575.symmetry_origin: Unitary invariance $\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{H})$: the von Neumann entropy is invariant under arbitrary unitary transformations $\rho \mapsto U \rho U^\dagger$, preserving the eigenspectrum of the density matrix.
shared-information-384ac575.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of maximal mixing in a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space, $\rho \to \frac{1}{d}\mathbb{I}$, the entropy reaches its maximum $S(\rho) = \ln d$. For any pure state projection $\rho^2 = \rho$, the purity satisfies $\gamma = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho^2) = 1$, yielding the absolute global minimum of entropy $S(\rho) = 0$.
shared-information-384ac575.conceptual_definition: For a quantum system described by a density operator $\rho$, the von Neumann entropy is defined as $S(\rho) = -\mathrm{Tr}(\rho \ln \rho)$. When the state is pure, the density operator acts as a rank-one projection operator $\rho = |\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$, whose spectrum consists of a single non-zero eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 1$ and all other eigenvalues $\lambda_{k>1} = 0$. Consequently, evaluating the trace over the spectral decomposition yields $S(\rho) = -(1 \ln 1 + \sum 0 \ln 0) = 0$.
shared-information-384ac575.intuitive_summary: In quantum mechanics, a pure state represents maximal possible knowledge about the system; because there is zero statistical mixedness or classical uncertainty, its information-theoretic entropy is strictly zero.
shared-information-384ac575.description: The von Neumann entropy evaluates to identically zero for any pure quantum state, reflecting the complete absence of classical statistical uncertainty or missing information in an isolated quantum system described by a single state vector.

The right side of the equation, $\iint_{\Sigma}$ ( $

Integrating this projection over the entire surface \Sigma yields the total flux of the curl through the surface. Stokes' Theorem states that these two seemingly different quantities are equivalent$.
integral-geometric-identity-e2f9202c.symmetry_origin: Stokes' Theorem is a fundamental result in vector calculus and differential geometry. It arises from the generalized Stokes' theorem, which states that for an n-1 form $\omega$ and an n-dimensional manifold M with boundary $\partial M$, $\int_M d\omega = ∫_{\partial M} \omega$. In the case of vector calculus in three dimensions, $\mathbf{A} can be associated with a 1-form, and its curl \nabla \times \mathbf{A}$ is related to the exterior derivative of this 1-form. The theorem fundamentally relates the integral of a differential form over a manifold to the integral of its exterior derivative over the boundary of the manifold. This is a manifestation of the divergence theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus in higher dimensions, reflecting the underlying geometric structure of vector fields and their derivatives.
integral-geometric-identity-e2f9202c.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the surface $\Sigma$ shrinks to a point, both sides of the equation approach zero. This behavior is consistent with the interpretation of the curl as a measure of local rotation. When the vector field $\mathbf{A}$ is irrotational (i.e., $\nabla \times$ A = 0$), the surface integral is zero, implying that the line integral around any closed loop is also zero, meaning \mathbf{A} is a conservative field. Conversely, if the line integral around every possible closed loop is zero, then the curl must be zero everywhere$.
integral-geometric-identity-e2f9202c.conceptual_definition: The Integral Geometric Identity, also known as Stokes' Theorem in its vector calculus form, establishes a fundamental relationship between the line integral of a vector field along a closed curve and the surface integral of the curl of that same vector field over any surface bounded by that curve. It is a generalization of the fundamental theorem of calculus to higher dimensions.
integral-geometric-identity-e2f9202c.intuitive_summary: The total 'circulation' of a vector field around a boundary loop is equal to the total 'swirl' of the field passing through the surface enclosed by that loop.

branes-mass-relation-a49ef49d.symmetry_origin: Originates from 1/2-BPS supersymmetry saturation in extended supergravity, where the central charge of the supersymmetry algebra determines the mass-to-volume ratio.
branes-mass-relation-a49ef49d.limits_and_boundary: In the weak string coupling limit ($g_s \to 0$), the mass diverges as $M_p \to \infty$, rendering D-branes infinitely heavy and rigid (non-perturbative sector). In the point-like limit ($V_p \to 0$ for $p > 0$), $M_p \to 0$ unless compactification radii vanish, inducing T-duality transformations.
branes-mass-relation-a49ef49d.conceptual_definition: In superstring theory, a Dirichlet $p$-brane (D$p$-brane) is an extended, non-perturbative dynamical hypersurface of spatial dimension $p$. The mass $M_p$ of a static, flat D$p$-brane wrapped over a compact or finite spatial cycle of volume $V_p$ scales proportionally to the volume and inversely with the dimensionless string coupling constant $g_s$, reflecting the tension behavior $T_p \propto 1/(g_s l_s^{p+1})$.
branes-mass-relation-a49ef49d.intuitive_summary: Because D-branes are non-perturbative solitonic objects in string theory, their mass diverges in the weak-coupling limit ($g_s \to 0$), scaling as $1/g_s$ rather than $1/g_s^2$ (which is characteristic of NS5-branes or closed string solitons), and grows linearly with the spatial volume they occupy.

quantum-bayes-rule-12c9d6a4.interpretation: The prior state is described by the statistical density operator $\rho_{\text{prior}}$, representing prior preparation or incomplete knowledge. The operator $P_m$ is an orthogonal projection operator ($P_m^2 = P_m = P_m^\dagger$) acting on the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ associated with measurement outcome $m$. The numerator $P_m \rho_{\text{prior}} P_m$ performs non-unitary state filtering (Lüders reduction), while the denominator $\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_{\text{prior}} P_m)$ supplies the necessary normalization constant so that $\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_{\text{post}}) = 1$.
quantum-bayes-rule-12c9d6a4.symmetry_origin: Convex geometry of the state space of positive trace-class operators and invariance under unitary transformation of the measurement basis.
quantum-bayes-rule-12c9d6a4.limits_and_boundary: When the measurement operator is rank-1 ($P_m = |m\rangle\langle m|$), the posterior state collapses entirely to the pure state $|m\rangle\langle m|$ regardless of whether $\rho_{\text{prior}}$ was mixed or pure. In the limit where $P_m$ is the identity operator $\mathbb{I}$, no measurement information is gained and $\rho_{\text{post}} = \rho_{\text{prior}}$. If $\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_{\text{prior}} P_m) = 0$, outcome $m$ is forbidden by the Born rule.
quantum-bayes-rule-12c9d6a4.conceptual_definition: The Quantum Bayes' Rule defines the transformation of an initial density operator $\rho_{\text{prior}}$ into a normalized posterior density operator $\rho_{\text{post}}$ conditional upon obtaining measurement outcome $m$ represented by the projection operator $P_m$. Mathematically, $\rho_{\text{post}} = \frac{P_m \rho_{\text{prior}} P_m}{\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_{\text{prior}} P_m)}$, where the denominator represents the Born rule probability $p(m) = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_{\text{prior}} P_m)$ of recording outcome $m$.
quantum-bayes-rule-12c9d6a4.intuitive_summary: Just as classical Bayes' theorem conditions a prior probability distribution on new evidence, Quantum Bayes' rule conditions a quantum state on a measurement outcome by projecting onto the eigenspace of that outcome and renormalizing the trace to unity.
quantum-bayes-rule-12c9d6a4.description: Formulates the state update of a quantum density operator following a projective measurement with an observed outcome, serving as the quantum operational analogue of classical Bayesian conditioning.

massless-scalar-propagator-pole-1105e1fb.title: Feynman Propagator for a Massless Scalar / Nambu-Goldstone Boson in Momentum Space
massless-scalar-propagator-pole-1105e1fb.interpretation: The quantity $D(p)$ denotes the Feynman propagator in momentum space. The variable $p$ represents the four-momentum vector with Minkowski invariant square $p^2 = p_\mu p^\mu = (p^0)^2 - |\mathbf{p}|^2$. The imaginary unit $i$ in the numerator arises from the canonical definition as a Green's function of the differential operator $\Box$. The infinitesimal term $+i\epsilon$ (where $\epsilon > 0$) displaces the physical poles into the complex energy plane, specifying the contour integral prescription that selects positive-frequency modes propagating forward in time and negative-frequency modes propagating backward in time.
massless-scalar-propagator-pole-1105e1fb.symmetry_origin: Originates from Poincaré invariance (Lorentz invariance and spacetime translational symmetry) of the massless Klein-Gordon action, alongside shift symmetry associated with spontaneously broken continuous global symmetries (Goldstone's theorem).
massless-scalar-propagator-pole-1105e1fb.limits_and_boundary: As $p^2 \to 0$ (on-shell limit), the propagator exhibits an isolated simple pole corresponding to the physical propagation of a massless particle on the light cone. In the ultraviolet limit $p^2 \to \infty$, the amplitude scales as $O(1/p^2)$, consistent with canonical power-counting in four spacetime dimensions. In the massive scalar propagator limit $m \to 0$, $D(p) = \frac{i}{p^2 - m^2 + i\epsilon} \to \frac{i}{p^2 + i\epsilon}$.

mass-proportionality-vev.title: Mass Proportionality to Vacuum Expectation Value
mass-proportionality-vev.conceptual_definition: In the Standard Model of particle physics, fundamental mass scales arise dynamically from the spontaneous breaking of the electroweak gauge group $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y \to U(1)_{\text{em}}$. The non-zero vacuum expectation value $v = \langle 0 | \Phi | 0 \rangle \approx 246.22\text{ GeV}$ sets the universal dimensionful scale for masses, such that both fermion masses $m_f = y_f v / \sqrt{2}$ (via Yukawa couplings) and vector gauge boson masses $M_W = g v / 2$ (via gauge covariant kinetic terms) exhibit the direct scaling relation $m_i \propto v$.
mass-proportionality-vev.intuitive_summary: The Higgs vacuum expectation value acts as a universal scale factor for inertia; empty space is filled with a uniform condensate, and a particle's mass is proportional to the product of this background field density and its intrinsic coupling to it.
mass-proportionality-vev.interpretation: The symbol $m_i$ denotes the pole mass of particle $i$ (fermion or gauge boson), and $v$ is the classical vacuum expectation value of the scalar field. The constant of proportionality is determined by the dimensionless coupling parameter specific to the interaction channel: the Yukawa coupling $y_i / \sqrt{2}$ for fundamental fermions, or gauge group coupling factors such as $g/2$ and $\sqrt{g^2 + g'^2}/2$ for the $W^\pm$ and $Z^0$ gauge bosons, respectively. If $v \to 0$, electroweak symmetry remains unbroken and all elementary fermions and gauge bosons become strictly massless.
mass-proportionality-vev.symmetry_origin: Spontaneous breakdown of the electroweak gauge symmetry $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ down to electromagnetic $U(1)_{\text{em}}$ triggered by the tachyonic mass term in the Higgs scalar potential.
mass-proportionality-vev.limits_and_boundary: In the symmetric phase limit $T > T_c$ (or at energy scales where $v \to 0$), all particle masses $m_i \to 0$, restoring full electroweak gauge invariance. In the decoupling limit where $y_i \to 0$, the mass $m_i \to 0$ even in the broken phase.

symmetry-metric-tensor.title: Symmetry of Metric Tensor
symmetry-metric-tensor.conceptual_definition: The symmetry of the metric tensor, represented by the equation $g^{\mu u} = g^{ u\mu}$, signifies that the components of the contravariant metric tensor are symmetric. The metric tensor is a fundamental object in differential geometry and general relativity that defines the metric (or distance) in a given spacetime manifold. Its components dictate how to measure lengths, angles, and volumes within that manifold. The symmetry property means that swapping the indices $\mu$ and $u$ does not change the value of the component $g^{\mu u}$. This property is crucial for many calculations in physics, particularly in general relativity where it simplifies the Einstein field equations and ensures consistency in the geometric description of spacetime.
symmetry-metric-tensor.intuitive_summary: The relationship between any two spacetime directions is the same regardless of the order in which you consider them, as reflected by the symmetric nature of the metric tensor components.
symmetry-metric-tensor.interpretation: In this equation, $g^{\mu u}$ represents the components of the contravariant metric tensor. The indices $\mu$ and $u$ are spacetime indices, typically taking values 0, 1, 2, 3, where 0 usually denotes the time dimension and 1, 2, 3 denote the spatial dimensions. The equation $g^{\mu u} = g^{ u\mu}$ states that the component of the metric tensor with indices $\mu$ and $u$ is equal to the component with indices $u$ and $\mu$. This implies that the metric tensor is a symmetric tensor. For example, the component $g^{01}$ (relating time and the first spatial direction) is equal to $g^{10}$ (relating the first spatial direction and time). This symmetry is not an arbitrary choice but arises from the fundamental structure of spacetime and its description in terms of a metric. It ensures that the way distances and intervals are measured is consistent and independent of the order in which spatial or temporal components are combined.
symmetry-metric-tensor.symmetry_origin: The symmetry of the metric tensor $g^{\mu u} = g^{ u\mu}$ stems directly from the definition of the metric tensor itself in a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold. In these geometries, the metric tensor is constructed from an inner product on the tangent space, which is inherently symmetric. In the context of general relativity, the metric tensor is the fundamental object that encodes the gravitational field and the geometry of spacetime. Its symmetry is a necessary condition for it to represent a metric and is preserved under coordinate transformations. Furthermore, this symmetry is essential for ensuring that the laws of physics are independent of the observer's coordinate system (coordinate invariance). It also simplifies the derivation and form of the Einstein field equations, which relate the spacetime geometry (represented by the metric tensor) to the distribution of matter and energy.
symmetry-metric-tensor.limits_and_boundary: This equation describes a fundamental property of the metric tensor in any dimension and under any curvature conditions. Therefore, it does not have 'limits' in the sense of variables approaching zero or infinity that would change the symmetry condition itself. The values of the components $g^{\mu u}$ can vary widely depending on the spacetime curvature (e.g., approaching zero in regions of extreme gravity or maintaining certain values in flat spacetime), but their symmetric relationship $g^{\mu u} = g^{ u\mu}$ remains invariant.

field-commutation-spacelike.title: Microcausality Condition for Spacelike-Separated Local Field Operators
field-commutation-spacelike.conceptual_definition: In relativistic quantum field theory, the microcausality (or Einstein causality) condition requires that any two local gauge-invariant or bosonic field observables $\mathcal{A}(x)$ and $\mathcal{B}(y)$ commute when their spacetime separation is spacelike, $(x - y)^2 < 0$ (under the mostly-minus metric signature $\\beta = \operatorname{diag}(+1, -1, -1, -1)$). This ensures the relativistic prohibition of superluminal signaling and preserves quantum mechanical measurement compatibility at spacelike distances.
field-commutation-spacelike.intuitive_summary: Events separated by more space than light can traverse cannot affect each other; thus, performing a measurement at point $x$ does not disturb a simultaneous or spacelike measurement at point $y$.
field-commutation-spacelike.interpretation: The equation $[\mathcal{A}(x), \mathcal{B}(y)] = \mathcal{A}(x)\mathcal{B}(y) - \mathcal{B}(y)\mathcal{A}(x) = 0$ dictates that the commutator of field operators $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$, evaluated at distinct four-vectors $x^\mu$ and $y^\mu$, vanishes identically whenever $(x - y)^2 < 0$. Consequently, localized physical operations or measurements represented by these operators are mutually independent and can be simultaneously diagonalized.
field-commutation-spacelike.symmetry_origin: Rooted in proper orthochronous Poincaré invariance $\mathrm{SO}^+(1,3) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^{1,3}$ and the geometric structure of Minkowski spacetime, specifically preserving causality under Lorentz boosts.
field-commutation-spacelike.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit $c \to \infty$, the spacelike light cone opens completely, and this condition reduces to the standard equal-time commutation of distinct spatial coordinates $[\hat{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{x}, t), \hat{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{y}, t)] = 0$ for $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{y}$. For timelike separations $(x - y)^2 > 0$, the commutator is generally non-zero due to causal propagation governed by the retarded Green's function.

luminosity-accretion.title: Accretion Luminosity of a White Dwarf
luminosity-accretion.conceptual_definition: The accretion luminosity $L = \frac{G M_{\text{WD}} \dot{M}}{R_{\text{WD}}}$ quantifies the rate of gravitational binding energy liberated per unit time when matter falls from asymptotic infinity ($\Phi \to 0$) to the stellar surface at radius $R_{\text{WD}}$. Assuming the total kinetic energy acquired during infall is completely thermalized and radiated at the boundary layer or disk surface, the output power directly scales with the deep gravitational well of the compact degenerate core and the mass transfer rate $\dot{M}$.
luminosity-accretion.intuitive_summary: As gas falls deep into the gravitational well of a dense white dwarf, it gains kinetic energy that converts into heat and intense electromagnetic radiation upon striking the surface or inner accretion disk.
luminosity-accretion.interpretation: The total luminosity $L$ (expressed in $\text{W}$) represents the emitted electromagnetic power. The term $\frac{G M_{\text{WD}}}{R_{\text{WD}}}$ represents the gravitational potential difference per unit mass between infinity and the surface of a compact object of mass $M_{\text{WD}}$ (in $\text{kg}$) and radius $R_{\text{WD}}$ (in $\text{m}$), where $G$ is Newton's gravitational constant ($\text{m}^3\text{ kg}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-2}$). Multiplying this gravitational potential by the mass accretion rate $\dot{M} = \frac{dM}{dt}$ (in $\text{kg s}^{-1}$) yields the radiated mechanical energy flux under the assumption of complete radiative dissipation.
luminosity-accretion.symmetry_origin: Conservation of total energy (Noetherian invariance under continuous time translations $t \to t + \epsilon$), governing the conversion of gravitational potential energy into radiative kinetic and thermal energy.
luminosity-accretion.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of vanishing mass transfer $\dot{M} \to 0$, accretion luminosity vanishes $L \to 0$. As $R_{\text{WD}} \to \infty$, the gravitational well flattens and potential release per unit mass approaches zero. When $L$ approaches the Eddington luminosity limit $L_{\text{Edd}} = \frac{4\pi G M c}{\kappa}$, radiation pressure balances gravitational attraction, halting steady infall.

lagrangian-symplectic-form.title: Lagrangian Symplectic Form
lagrangian-symplectic-form.conceptual_definition: The symplectic form $\Omega$ is a non-degenerate, closed differential 2-form defined on the cotangent bundle $T^*Q$ (or the tangent bundle $T Q$ via the Legendre transform). It is generated by taking the exterior derivative of the canonical (tautological) 1-form $\theta = \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \mathrm{d}q^i$, yielding $\Omega = \mathrm{d}\theta = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{d}p_i \wedge \mathrm{d}q^i$. This form induces an isomorphism between the tangent and cotangent bundles, furnishing the phase space with a symplectic manifold structure.
lagrangian-symplectic-form.intuitive_summary: The symplectic form measures oriented phase-space area per degree of freedom, serving as the fundamental geometric arena where energy gradients translate into physical equations of motion.
lagrangian-symplectic-form.interpretation: The 2-form $\Omega$ endows phase space with a non-degenerate, skew-symmetric bilinear structure. The canonical 1-form $\theta = \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \mathrm{d}q^i$ pairs each generalized momentum $p_i$ with the infinitesimal coordinate variation $\mathrm{d}q^i$. Taking the exterior derivative $\mathrm{d}$ yields $\Omega = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{d}p_i \wedge \mathrm{d}q^i$, where the nilpotency $\mathrm{d}^2 = 0$ guarantees that $\Omega$ is automatically closed ($\mathrm{d}\Omega = 0$). Non-degeneracy ensures that for every Hamiltonian $H$, there is a uniquely defined vector field $X_H$ satisfying $\iota_{X_H}\Omega = \mathrm{d}H$.
lagrangian-symplectic-form.symmetry_origin: Rooted in the diffeomorphism invariance of the underlying configuration manifold $Q$ lifted to the cotangent bundle $T^*Q$, and invariant under symplectomorphisms generated by canonical transformations and Hamiltonian flows (Liouville's theorem).
lagrangian-symplectic-form.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, quantum commutators $[\hat{q}^i, \hat{p}_j] = i\hbar \delta^i_j$ asymptotically map to the Poisson brackets induced by the inverse of $\Omega$. For degenerate Lagrangians (Dirac constraint theory), $\Omega$ pulls back to a presymplectic form with a non-trivial kernel.

jacobi-metric-alternative.title: Jacobi Metric (Alternative Form)
jacobi-metric-alternative.conceptual_definition: The Jacobi metric reformulates Maupertuis' principle of stationary action into the differential geometry of geodesics. For a system with configuration space metric $g_{ij}$, total energy $E$, and potential energy $V(q)$, the physical trajectories traced out in configuration space are unparameterized geodesics with respect to the conformally scaled metric tensor $\tilde{g}_{ij} = 2(E - V(q)) g_{ij}$.
jacobi-metric-alternative.intuitive_summary: Classical mechanics in a potential field is mathematically equivalent to free particle motion (geodesic flow) on a curved manifold whose distance element is stretched by the local kinetic energy.
jacobi-metric-alternative.interpretation: The line element squared $ds^2$ represents the infinitesimal geometric distance along a trajectory in configuration space. The factor $2(E - V)$ is twice the available kinetic energy $T = E - V(q)$, acting as a conformal scaling factor. The tensor $g_{ij}$ is the mass or kinematic metric of the configuration space, and $dq^i, dq^j$ represent the differential coordinate displacements with implicit Einstein summation over indices $i, j$.
jacobi-metric-alternative.symmetry_origin: Time-translation invariance guarantees the conservation of total energy $E = T + V$, enabling the reparameterization of time $t$ in terms of the geometric arc length $s$.
jacobi-metric-alternative.limits_and_boundary: At classical turning points where $E = V(q)$, the metric degenerates ($ds \to 0$), corresponding to the boundary of the classically accessible region. In regions where $V(q) = 0$ (free particle), the Jacobi metric reduces to a constant scalar multiple of the kinetic configuration metric $2E g_{ij}$.

baryon-number-assignment.title: Baryon Number Assignment for Single Baryons
baryon-number-assignment.conceptual_definition: The baryon number $B$ is an additive conserved quantum number defined as $B = \frac{1}{3}(n_q - n_{\b\bar{q}}})$, where $n_q$ is the number of valence quarks and $n_{\b\bar{q}}}$ is the number of valence antiquarks. For a conventional colour-singlet baryon composed of three quarks ($q q q$), the total baryon number evaluates identically to $B = 1$.
baryon-number-assignment.intuitive_summary: Each quark contributes one-third of a unit of baryonic charge, so three quarks bound together naturally make a single baryon with $B=1$.
baryon-number-assignment.interpretation: In this definition, $B$ denotes the global additive baryon quantum number. A value of $B = 1$ is universally assigned to all color-singlet triquark bound states, such as protons ($p$), neutrons ($n$), and hyperons (e.g., $\Lambda$, $\Sigma$, $\Xi$, $\Omega$). Antiquarks carry $B = -1/3$ and leptons/mesons carry $B = 0$, ensuring this discrete value identifies single baryonic matter states.
baryon-number-assignment.symmetry_origin: Associated with the accidental global $U(1)_B$ phase transformation symmetry of the Standard Model Lagrangian: $q_i \to e^{i \alpha / 3} q_i$.
baryon-number-assignment.limits_and_boundary: Strictly conserved in classical perturbative Standard Model interactions. Broken non-perturbatively by the chiral anomaly via electroweak sphalerons at high temperatures ($T \gtrsim 100\text{ GeV}$) or in Grand Unified Theories (GUTs) via $X$ and $Y$ gauge boson exchange.

triangle-inequality-for-metric.title: Triangle Inequality for a Distance Metric
triangle-inequality-for-metric.conceptual_definition: For any set $M$ equipped with a metric $\tau: M \times M \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, the triangle inequality dictates that for all elements $A, B, C \in M$, the distance function satisfies $\tau(A, C) \le \tau(A, B) + \tau(B, C)$. This serves as one of the defining axioms of metric spaces and Riemannian manifolds.
triangle-inequality-for-metric.intuitive_summary: The shortest path between two points is the direct route; visiting an intermediate waypoint cannot reduce the total distance traveled.
triangle-inequality-for-metric.interpretation: In this relation, $\tau(A, C)$ represents the metric separation between elements $A$ and $C$, while $\tau(A, B)$ and $\tau(B, C)$ represent the respective distances from $A$ to an intermediate element $B$ and from $B$ to $C$. The inequality ensures topological coherence and well-defined geodesic distances.
triangle-inequality-for-metric.symmetry_origin: Translational and rotational invariance in homogeneous metric spaces; fundamental axiom of metric topology.
triangle-inequality-for-metric.limits_and_boundary: Equality $\tau(A, C) = \tau(A, B) + \tau(B, C)$ holds if and only if $B$ lies on a metric geodesic directly connecting $A$ and $C$. If $A = B$ or $B = C$, the relation reduces trivially to an identity.

commutation-relation-spatially-separated.title: Microcausality Condition for Spacelike Separated Local Operators
commutation-relation-spatially-separated.conceptual_definition: In relativistic quantum field theory, the microcausality (or Einstein causality) axiom requires that any two local observable operators $\mathcal{O}_1(x)$ and $\mathcal{O}_2(y)$ commute when their spacetime arguments $x$ and $y$ are spacelike separated, satisfying $(x - y)^2 < 0$ (in mostly-plus metric signature) or $(x - y)^2 > 0$ (in mostly-minus). Mathematically, $[\mathcal{O}_1(x), \mathcal{O}_2(y)] = \mathcal{O}_1(x)\mathcal{O}_2(y) - \mathcal{O}_2(y)\mathcal{O}_1(x) = 0$, guaranteeing that a measurement at point $x$ cannot influence an event at spacelike-separated point $y$, thus preventing superluminal signaling.
commutation-relation-spatially-separated.intuitive_summary: Because information cannot travel faster than light, performing an experiment or measurement at one location cannot instantaneously disturb or affect the outcome of a measurement performed at a distant location outside its light cone.
commutation-relation-spatially-separated.interpretation: The expression $[\mathcal{O}_1(x), \mathcal{O}_2(y)] = 0$ is the commutator of two local operators. The symbol $\mathcal{O}_1(x)$ represents a local quantum field operator acting on the Hilbert space at spacetime event $x = (t_x, \mathbf{x})$, while $\mathcal{O}_2(y)$ represents a local operator at spacetime event $y = (t_y, \mathbf{y})$. When $(x - y)^2 < 0$, the interval is spacelike, implying that no physical signal moving at or below the speed of light $c$ can connect the two events. Vanishing commutator means both observables are simultaneously diagonalizable and represent compatible physical measurements without mutual quantum interference.
commutation-relation-spatially-separated.symmetry_origin: Lorentz Invariance and Relativistic Microcausality (Wightman Axioms)
commutation-relation-spatially-separated.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit $c \to \infty$, the light cone opens to the entire spacelike hyperplane, reducing microcausality to the standard equal-time commutation relations of quantum mechanics where spatial separation $|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}| > 0$ yields $[\mathcal{O}_1(\mathbf{x}, t), \mathcal{O}_2(\mathbf{y}, t)] = 0$. For timelike or lightlike separations $(x - y)^2 \ge 0$, the commutator is generally non-zero, allowing causal propagation described by advanced and retarded propagators.

motional-electromotive-force.title: Motional electromotive force
motional-electromotive-force.conceptual_definition: The formula for motional electromotive force (emf) is a generalization of Faraday's law of induction, specifically addressing the emf induced in a moving conductor within a magnetic field. It is derived from the Lorentz force experienced by charges within the conductor. The integral represents the work done per unit charge on charges as they move along a closed path within the conductor in the presence of both an electric field and a magnetic field. This work done is the emf.
motional-electromotive-force.intuitive_summary: The emf induced in a moving conductor is the sum of the electric potential difference due to the conductor's motion through a magnetic field and any existing electric field along the conductor.
motional-electromotive-force.interpretation: The equation ⁡⁡ = ∫ (⁡ + ⁡ × ⁡) ⋅ d⁡ defines the total electromotive force (⁡) induced in a closed path (∫ ... d⁡) around a conductor. ⁡ represents the electric field (⁡/⁡) present along the path. ⁡ is the velocity of the conductor (⁡/⁡), and ⁡ is the magnetic field (⁡/⁡⁡). The term ⁡ × ⁡ represents the magnetic force per unit charge on charges moving with velocity ⁡ in the magnetic field ⁡, and is often referred to as the motional electric field. The dot product with the differential length element d⁡ integrates this force per unit charge along the path, yielding the total work done per unit charge, which is the emf. This equation quantifies how a moving conductor, interacting with a magnetic field, can generate a voltage (emf), a phenomenon crucial for electric generators.
motional-electromotive-force.symmetry_origin: This formula originates from the fundamental Lorentz force law, ⁡ = ⁡(⁡ + ⁡ × ⁡), which describes the force on a charge ⁡ moving with velocity ⁡ in electric field ⁡ and magnetic field ⁡. The emf is defined as the work done per unit charge to move a charge around a closed loop, which is the line integral of the effective electric field along that loop. In this context, the "effective" electric field includes the contribution from the magnetic field's effect on moving charges, ⁡ × ⁡. The path independence of the electrostatic potential is violated when magnetic fields are present and changing, or when conductors are moving, leading to a non-conservative effective electric field and thus a non-zero emf around a closed loop.
motional-electromotive-force.limits_and_boundary: If the conductor is stationary (⁡ = 0), the formula simplifies to ⁡ = ∫ ⁡ ⋅ d⁡, which is the emf due to a static electric field. If there is no electric field (⁡ = 0) and the conductor is stationary (⁡ = 0), then the emf is zero (⁡ = 0), as expected. In the limit of a very strong magnetic field or very high velocity, the motional electric field term (⁡ × ⁡) will dominate the contributions to the emf, assuming a non-zero electric field is not present.

gradient-of-a-scalar-field-0c45fd93.title: Gradient of a Scalar Field
gradient-of-a-scalar-field-0c45fd93.description: This equation represents the gradient of a scalar field, indicating the direction and magnitude of the field's steepest increase.
gradient-of-a-scalar-field-0c45fd93.conceptual_definition: In physics, the gradient of a scalar field $\phi (denoted \nabla \phi)$ is a vector field that points in the direction of the greatest rate of increase of $\phi$. Its magnitude is the maximum rate of change of the scalar field. It is a fundamental operation in vector calculus, crucial for understanding how scalar quantities vary in space.
gradient-of-a-scalar-field-0c45fd93.interpretation:
Physically, 
\nabla $\phi$ describes how a scalar quantity, such as electric potential, gravitational potential, or temperature, changes across different spatial points. For instance, if $\phi$ is a potential energy, then - 
\nabla $\phi$ represents the conservative force acting on a particle. In the context of the 'Gravity Gap' formula, where $\phi$ likely represents a gravitational potential, its gradient 
\nabla $\phi$ would be directly related to the gravitational field or acceleration. It quantifies the spatial variation of the potential, indicating regions of stronger or weaker influence.
gradient-of-a-scalar-field-0c45fd93.limits_and_boundary: The gradient operation is well-defined for continuously differentiable scalar fields. Its behavior at boundaries depends on the specific boundary conditions imposed on the scalar field $\phi$. For example, if $\phi$ represents a potential, its gradient might vanish at points of equilibrium or be constant in regions of uniform field.
gradient-of-a-scalar-field-0c45fd93.symmetry_origin: The gradient operation itself doesn't inherently imply specific symmetries, but the scalar field $\phi$ it acts upon often arises from systems with underlying symmetries. For instance, if $\phi$ is spherically symmetric, its gradient will be purely radial. If $\phi$ is invariant under certain transformations, its gradient will reflect those symmetries in its spatial variation.

canonical-momentum-component-8b6f59f2.title: Canonical Momentum Component
canonical-momentum-component-8b6f59f2.description: Represents the $j$-th component of generalized (canonical) momentum conjugate to generalized coordinate $q_j$ in Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics.
canonical-momentum-component-8b6f59f2.conceptual_definition: The canonical momentum component $p_j$ is defined as the functional derivative or partial derivative of the Lagrangian $L(q, \dot{q}, t)$ with respect to the generalized velocity $\dot{q}_j$, expressed as $p_j = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j}$. In phase-space dynamics, it serves as the conjugate variable to $q_j$, forming the canonical pair $(q_j, p_j)$ governed by Hamilton's equations of motion.
canonical-momentum-component-8b6f59f2.interpretation: The component $p_j$ quantifies the rate of change of the system's action with respect to variation in the coordinate $q_j$. Unlike standard kinetic momentum $m v_j$, the canonical momentum includes potential field contributions, such as the electromagnetic vector potential term $q A_j$. In quantum mechanics, $p_j$ corresponds to the self-adjoint differential operator $\hat{p}_j = -i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial q_j}$.
canonical-momentum-component-8b6f59f2.limits_and_boundary: In the classical non-relativistic limit with velocity-independent potentials, $p_j \to m \dot{q}_j$. In quantum-to-classical correspondence ($\hbar \to 0$), the quantum operator expectation value $\langle \hat{p}_j \rangle$ asymptotically converges to the classical canonical momentum variable $p_j$ by the Ehrenfest theorem.
canonical-momentum-component-8b6f59f2.symmetry_origin: Via Noether's theorem, invariance of the Lagrangian under spatial translation along the generalized coordinate $q_j$ ensures that the conjugate canonical momentum $p_j$ is a strictly conserved quantity ($\dot{p}_j = 0$).

p_j.name: Canonical Momentum Component
p_j.description: The $j$-th component of canonical or generalized momentum conjugate to generalized coordinate $q_j$

canonical-momentum-component-8b6f59f2.intuitive_summary: Canonical momentum measures the dynamical inertia and generalized flow along a chosen coordinate direction, incorporating both mechanical motion and velocity-dependent potential interactions.

antibaryon-number-density-95dbb2dd.title: Antibaryon Number Density
antibaryon-number-density-95dbb2dd.description: Quantifies the local spatial number density of antibaryons within a given volume, derived from the phase-space distribution of antimatter composite hadrons carrying negative baryon number.
antibaryon-number-density-95dbb2dd.conceptual_definition: The antibaryon number density, denoted $n_{\b\bar{B}}}$, is the zeroth component of the conserved or quasi-conserved antibaryonic number current. In thermal field theory and statistical mechanics, it is calculated as the momentum-space integral of the Fermi-Dirac distribution function corresponding to antibaryonic states with chemical potential $\mu_{\b\bar{B}}} = -\mu_B$, summing over all composite antiquark spin and flavor states.
antibaryon-number-density-95dbb2dd.interpretation: In physical cosmology and relativistic heavy-ion collisions, $n_{\b\bar{B}}}$ tracks the abundance of antibaryons. Combined with the baryon number density $n_B$, it governs the net baryon number density $n_B - n_{\b\bar{B}}}$. In a symmetric universe or high-temperature quark-gluon plasma where the baryon chemical potential vanishes ($\mu_B = 0$), matter and antimatter densities are equal ($n_B = n_{\b\bar{B}}}$). In the late universe, baryogenesis leads to $n_{\b\bar{B}}} \approx 0$, leaving an asymmetry dominated by $n_B$.
antibaryon-number-density-95dbb2dd.limits_and_boundary: At zero temperature ($T \to 0$) in the presence of positive baryon chemical potential ($\mu_B > 0$), $n_{\b\bar{B}}} \to 0$ exponentially due to Boltzmann suppression. In the ultra-relativistic limit ($T \gg m_B, \mu_B \to 0$), $n_{\b\bar{B}}} \approx n_B \propto T^3$.
antibaryon-number-density-95dbb2dd.symmetry_origin: Associated with the global $U(1)_B$ baryon number symmetry of the Standard Model Lagrangian via Noether's theorem, where antibaryons carry charge $B = -1$.

n_{\\bar{B}}.description: Total volumetric number density of antibaryons

antibaryon-number-density-95dbb2dd.intuitive_summary: It measures the volumetric concentration of antimatter baryons (such as antiprotons and antineutrons), which when subtracted from the baryon density yields the net matter-antimatter asymmetry of the system.

constant-radial-coordinate-definition-35.title: Constant Radial Coordinate Constraint Definition
constant-radial-coordinate-definition-35.description: Defines a geometric holonomic constraint where the variable scalar radial coordinate $r$ is restricted to a fixed constant radius $R$, defining a spherical surface or circular cross-section.
constant-radial-coordinate-definition-35.conceptual_definition: The equation $r = R$ constitutes a 1-dimensional holonomic constraint on a coordinate manifold parameterized by spherical or cylindrical coordinates. By constraining the radial degree of freedom $r$ to a fixed value $R$, it establishes a submanifold $\mathcal{M}_{\text{sub}} \subset \mathcal{M}$ (such as an embedded 2-sphere $S^2$ within $\mathbb{R}^3$ or a spatial hypersurface in general relativity), reducing the spatial degrees of freedom by one and fixing the metric components accordingly.
constant-radial-coordinate-definition-35.interpretation: In this definition, $r$ represents the radial coordinate denoting the Euclidean or areal distance from the origin in spherical or cylindrical polar coordinates. The parameter $R$ is a constant real value with units of length representing the fixed radius. Setting $r = R$ implies that the differential displacement satisfies $dr = 0$, causing any radial kinetic energy terms or metric differentials $g_{rr} dr^2$ to vanish.
constant-radial-coordinate-definition-35.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $R \to 0$, the manifold collapses to a single coordinate point (the origin). In the asymptotic limit $R \to \infty$, the surface local curvature vanishes relative to macroscopic coordinate scales, approaching planar geometry over localized patches.
constant-radial-coordinate-definition-35.symmetry_origin: Invariance under spatial rotations $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ on a spherical shell or $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ along a circular path, reflecting spherical or axial geometric symmetry.

constant-radial-coordinate-definition-35.intuitive_summary: Fixing the radial distance to a constant locks the system onto a shell or circular path of fixed radius, simplifying 3D problems to 2D surfaces.

recoil-velocity-component-8591d3b5.title: Emitter Recoil Velocity Component
recoil-velocity-component-8591d3b5.description: Quantifies the line-of-sight component of the recoil velocity imparted to an emitting system (such as an atom or nucleus) during photon emission or particle ejection to conserve linear momentum.
recoil-velocity-component-8591d3b5.conceptual_definition: The recoil velocity component $v_{\text{rec}}$ describes the projection of the velocity acquired by an emitter of rest mass $M$ along the observer's line of sight as a consequence of momentum conservation during photon or particle emission. For a photon of energy $E_\gamma = \hbar \omega$, conservation of linear momentum demands $\mathbf{p}_{\text{rec}} = -\hbar \mathbf{k}$, leading to a non-relativistic recoil velocity magnitude of $v_{\text{rec}} = \frac{E_\gamma}{M c}$, which alters the emitted radiation frequency via the Doppler effect.
recoil-velocity-component-8591d3b5.interpretation: The parameter $v_{\text{rec}}$ represents the kinematic recoil velocity vector projected onto the observation axis. In atomic and nuclear spectroscopy (e.g., the Mössbauer effect), when a photon of momentum $p_\gamma = \frac{h}{\lambda}$ is emitted, the recoil momentum $M v_{\text{rec}}$ reduces the energy available to the photon by an amount $\Delta E_{\text{rec}} = \frac{1}{2} M v_{\text{rec}}^2 = \frac{E_\gamma^2}{2 M c^2}$. A positive $v_{\text{rec}}$ along the line of sight indicates motion away from the detector, inducing an additional Doppler redshift.
recoil-velocity-component-8591d3b5.limits_and_boundary: In the macroscopic or crystal lattice limit ($M \to \infty$), $v_{\text{rec}} \to 0$, eliminating recoil losses as seen in recoilless nuclear resonance fluorescence (Mössbauer effect). In the ultra-relativistic limit where $E_\gamma \sim M c^2$, relativistic momentum $p = \gamma M v_{\text{rec}}$ must be used, ensuring $v_{\text{rec}} < c$.
recoil-velocity-component-8591d3b5.symmetry_origin: Spatial translation invariance (via Noether's theorem), which enforces the conservation of total linear momentum between the emitting body and the emitted radiation.

v_{rec}.name: recoil velocity component
v_{rec}.description: Line-of-sight velocity component imparted to the emitter due to momentum recoil upon emission

recoil-velocity-component-8591d3b5.intuitive_summary: Just as a cannon recoils backward when firing a cannonball, an atom recoils backward when emitting a photon, shifting the photon's observed frequency slightly to the red.

electrostatic-potential-inverse-distance.title: Inverse Distance Proportionality of the Electrostatic Potential
electrostatic-potential-inverse-distance.description: States that the electrostatic scalar potential generated by an isolated localized charge distribution scales inversely with radial distance in three-dimensional Euclidean space.
electrostatic-potential-inverse-distance.conceptual_definition: The electrostatic potential $V(r)$ generated by a spherically symmetric or localized point source of charge in three spatial dimensions obeys an inverse-distance scaling relation $V(r) \propto 1/r$. This behavior represents the fundamental Green's function solution to Laplace's equation $\nabla^2 V = 0$ outside the source region under the boundary condition that the potential vanishes at spatial infinity ($V \to 0$ as $r \to \infty$).
electrostatic-potential-inverse-distance.interpretation: The quantity $V(r)$ denotes the electric scalar potential as a function of radial coordinate $r$. The proportionality $V(r) \propto 1/r$ highlights the monopolar dominance in the multipole expansion of electrostatic systems. The radial coordinate $r = \|\mathbf{r}\|$ measures the Euclidean distance from the center of the charge distribution. The potential difference between infinity and $r$ directly quantifies the work required per unit test charge to bring a particle from infinity to distance $r$.
electrostatic-potential-inverse-distance.limits_and_boundary: As $r \to \infty$, the potential asymptotically vanishes ($V(r) \to 0$), satisfying standard Dirichlet boundary conditions at infinity for isolated systems. As $r \to 0$, the classical potential exhibits an unphysical Coulomb singularity ($V(r) \to \pm \infty$), which in realistic physics is regularized by finite charge distributions, quantum electrodynamic vacuum polarization, or charge-smearing effects.
electrostatic-potential-inverse-distance.symmetry_origin: $SO(3)$ spatial rotational invariance and the translation invariance of free three-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^3$, linked with the scale invariance of the massless Poisson equation $\nabla^2 V = 0$.

V.name: Electrostatic Potential
V.description: Scalar electric potential evaluated at distance $r$

r.description: Euclidean radial distance from the source charge

electrostatic-potential-inverse-distance.intuitive_summary: In three-dimensional space, the geometric surface area of a sphere grows as $r^2$, spreading the flux of the electric field over an area that dilutes as $1/r^2$. Integrating this field radially yields a potential that drops off inversely with the first power of distance, $1/r$.

riemann-curvature-tensor-definition-7138.title: Riemann Curvature Tensor Definition
riemann-curvature-tensor-definition-7138.description: This equation defines the Riemann curvature tensor, a fundamental object in differential geometry and general relativity, in terms of Christoffel symbols and their derivatives. It quantifies the intrinsic curvature of a manifold.
riemann-curvature-tensor-definition-7138.conceptual_definition: The Riemann curvature tensor measures the failure of parallel transport of a vector around an infinitesimal closed loop to return to its original orientation. It is a (1,3)-tensor field that captures the intrinsic curvature of a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold. Its components are expressed using Christoffel symbols, which encode the metric's derivatives and define the connection.
riemann-curvature-tensor-definition-7138.interpretation: Physically, the Riemann curvature tensor describes the tidal forces experienced by objects in a gravitational field, which are a manifestation of spacetime curvature. In a flat spacetime (or Euclidean space), all components of the Riemann tensor are zero, meaning vectors can be parallel transported without changing their direction relative to the manifold. A non-zero Riemann tensor indicates that spacetime is curved, causing geodesics to converge or diverge, and affecting the relative acceleration of nearby particles.
riemann-curvature-tensor-definition-7138.limits_and_boundary: This formula is valid in any differentiable manifold equipped with a metric and a compatible connection (e.g., Levi-Civita connection). In the limit of flat spacetime, all Christoffel symbols and their derivatives vanish, leading to a zero Riemann tensor. It applies to both Riemannian and pseudo-Riemannian manifolds.
riemann-curvature-tensor-definition-7138.symmetry_origin: The Riemann tensor possesses several important symmetries: antisymmetry in the last two indices ($R^\rho_{\sigma\mu u} = -R^\rho_{\sigma u\mu}$), and the first Bianchi identity ($R^\rho_{\sigma\mu u} + R^\rho_{\mu u\sigma} + R^\rho_{ u\sigma\mu} = 0$). These symmetries arise from the properties of the connection and the underlying manifold structure.

chemical-potential-of-species-i-262d5ec6.title: Chemical Potential of Species i
chemical-potential-of-species-i-262d5ec6.description: This quantity represents the change in a system's Gibbs free energy when one mole of species 'i' is added at constant temperature and pressure.
chemical-potential-of-species-i-262d5ec6.conceptual_definition: The chemical potential $\mu_i$ quantifies the change in the system's energy when the number of particles of type $i$ is varied, while keeping other extensive variables (like volume or entropy) and other particle numbers constant. It is a partial molar quantity, specifically the partial molar Gibbs free energy, and acts as a driving force for particle diffusion and chemical reactions. In equilibrium, the chemical potential of a species is uniform throughout a system or equal across phases.
chemical-potential-of-species-i-262d5ec6.interpretation: Physically, $\mu_i$ can be thought of as the 'escaping tendency' of species $i$ from a phase. A higher chemical potential for a species in one region compared to another indicates a net flow of that species from the higher potential region to the lower potential region, driving the system towards equilibrium. It is a crucial concept in thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, and chemical kinetics, determining the direction of spontaneous processes involving particle transfer or chemical transformations. For the given master formula, $\mu_n = \mu_p + \mu_e$, it represents the chemical potential of neutrons, protons, and electrons, respectively, in a system at equilibrium.
chemical-potential-of-species-i-262d5ec6.limits_and_boundary: The concept of chemical potential is generally applicable to systems in thermodynamic equilibrium or quasi-static processes. It is well-defined for macroscopic systems where statistical mechanics applies. For ideal gases or dilute solutions, specific expressions for $\mu_i$ can be derived. At very low temperatures, quantum effects may become significant, altering the behavior of $\mu_i$.
chemical-potential-of-species-i-262d5ec6.symmetry_origin: The existence of chemical potential is deeply rooted in the conservation of particle number (or the ability to change particle number) and the second law of thermodynamics, which dictates the direction of spontaneous processes towards equilibrium. In systems where particle number is conserved, the chemical potential acts as a Lagrange multiplier associated with this constraint.

\\mu_i.name: \mu_i
\\mu_i.description: Chemical potential of species i (Joules per mole, J/mol)

condition-for-high-material-permeability.title: High Magnetic Permeability Regime Condition
condition-for-high-material-permeability.description: An inequality specifying the regime where the absolute magnetic permeability of a medium significantly exceeds the permeability of free space, characteristic of ferromagnetic and soft magnetic materials.
condition-for-high-material-permeability.conceptual_definition: The condition $\mu \gg \mu_0$ defines the strong magnetic response regime of matter, wherein the induced internal magnetization density $\mathbf{M}$ dominates over the vacuum displacement, causing the magnetic flux density $\mathbf{B}$ to be heavily concentrated within the medium for a given applied magnetic field strength $\mathbf{H}$.
condition-for-high-material-permeability.interpretation: The parameter $\mu$ represents the total absolute magnetic permeability of the medium, while $\mu_0$ is the vacuum magnetic permeability constant. Since the relationship is governed by $\mu = \mu_0 (1 + \chi_m)$, the inequality $\mu \gg \mu_0$ is mathematically equivalent to the magnetic susceptibility satisfying $\chi_m \gg 1$. This regime is essential for designing high-efficiency transformer cores, inductors, and magnetic shielding.
condition-for-high-material-permeability.limits_and_boundary: As temperature $T$ approaches and exceeds the Curie temperature $T_c$, spontaneous magnetic ordering vanishes and the material transitions into a paramagnetic phase where $\mu \to \mu_0$ and $\chi_m \ll 1$. At extreme applied magnetic fields $\mathbf{H} \to \infty$, domain magnetization saturates ($\|\mathbf{M}\| \to M_s$), causing the differential permeability $\mathrm{d}B/\mathrm{d}H$ to asymptotically approach $\mu_0$.
condition-for-high-material-permeability.symmetry_origin: Rooted in electromagnetic $U(1)$ gauge symmetry and spatial rotational invariance of isotropic constitutive media, combined with spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking at the microscopic level in ferromagnetic domains.

\\mu.description: The measure of the ability of a material to support the formation of a magnetic field within itself.

\\mu_0.name: Vacuum magnetic permeability

condition-for-high-material-permeability.intuitive_summary: In high-permeability materials, magnetic flux lines preferentially channel through the substance rather than surrounding space, behaving like a low-resistance path for magnetic circuits.

approach-to-schwarzschild-radius-from-ab.title: Asymptotic Exterior Approach to the Schwarzschild Event Horizon
approach-to-schwarzschild-radius-from-ab.description: Represents the one-sided limiting process where the areal radius coordinate $r$ approaches the Schwarzschild radius $r_s$ from the exterior spacetime domain $r > r_s$.
approach-to-schwarzschild-radius-from-ab.conceptual_definition: In the standard Schwarzschild coordinate chart $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, the limiting condition $r \to r_s^+$ characterizes the asymptotic boundary of the static exterior patch. Approaching $r_s$ from above reveals the coordinate singularity of the Schwarzschild metric where the temporal component $g_{tt} = -(1 - r_s/r) \to 0^-$ and the radial component $g_{rr} = (1 - r_s/r)^{-1} \to +\infty$, demonstrating infinite gravitational redshift and extreme time dilation relative to an asymptotic observer at spatial infinity.
approach-to-schwarzschild-radius-from-ab.interpretation: The parameter $r$ denotes the Schwarzschild radial coordinate (areal radius), defined such that spheres of constant $r$ have surface area $4\pi r^2$. The critical threshold $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ is the Schwarzschild radius associated with mass $M$. The notation $\to r_s^+$ explicitly enforces that the limit is taken exclusively through the exterior region $r > r_s$, ensuring proper evaluation of one-sided limits for physical quantities such as gravitational redshift factor $z = (1 - r_s/r)^{-1/2} - 1 \to \infty$ and proper acceleration $a = \frac{GM}{r^2\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}} \to \infty$ required for a stationary observer.
approach-to-schwarzschild-radius-from-ab.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $r \to r_s^+$, the redshift factor $1/\sqrt{-g_{tt}} \to \infty$ and the coordinate light cone tips asymptotically inward. In contrast, in the asymptotic limit $r \to \infty$, flat Minkowski spacetime $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ is recovered with $g_{tt} \to -1$ and $g_{rr} \to 1$.
approach-to-schwarzschild-radius-from-ab.symmetry_origin: Inherits the $SO(3)$ spatial spherical symmetry and $\mathbb{R}$ time-translation isometry generated by the timelike Killing vector field $\xi = \partial_t$ in the exterior static Schwarzschild manifold.

approach-to-schwarzschild-radius-from-ab.intuitive_summary: As an observer or light ray nears the event horizon from the outside, clocks appear to freeze and outgoing light is red-shifted to zero frequency from the perspective of distant observers.

position-dependent-vector-field-6644c96e.title: Position-Dependent Vector Field
position-dependent-vector-field-6644c96e.description: Represents a classical or continuum vector field mapping each spatial position vector to a corresponding physical vector quantity.
position-dependent-vector-field-6644c96e.conceptual_definition: A position-dependent vector field $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})$ is a smooth section of the tangent bundle or a vector-valued function $\mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ (or $\mathcal{M} \to T\mathcal{M}$) that assigns a unique vector $\mathbf{F}$ to each spatial point specified by the position vector $\mathbf{r} = (x, y, z)$.
position-dependent-vector-field-6644c96e.interpretation: The expression $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})$ represents a spatially varying vector quantity. The variable $\mathbf{r}$ denotes the position vector in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^3$, and $\mathbf{F}$ is the vector field evaluated at that specific coordinate. In classical mechanics and electrodynamics, $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})$ can represent static force fields, electric fields $\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r})$, magnetic fields $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r})$, or fluid velocity fields $\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r})$.
position-dependent-vector-field-6644c96e.limits_and_boundary: As $|\mathbf{r}| \to \infty$, localized physical fields typically decay to zero (e.g., $|\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})| = \mathcal{O}(r^{-2})$ for inverse-square fields). At isolated singular points (e.g., $|\mathbf{r}| \to 0$), the field may exhibit distributional singularities such as Dirac delta sources.
position-dependent-vector-field-6644c96e.symmetry_origin: Spatial translation and rotation invariance under the Euclidean group $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ or general covariance under diffeomorphism groups on smooth manifolds.

\\mathbf{F}.name: Vector Field
\\mathbf{F}.description: Physical vector-valued function evaluated at a given spatial location.

\\mathbf{r}.name: Position Vector
\\mathbf{r}.description: Spatial coordinate vector specifying the point of evaluation in space.

position-dependent-vector-field-6644c96e.intuitive_summary: At every location in space, a vector field places an arrow indicating both the magnitude and direction of a physical quantity, such as force, velocity, or electromagnetic field strength.

angular-wave-number-definition-1c8a7d35.title: Angular Wave Number Definition
angular-wave-number-definition-1c8a7d35.description: This equation defines the angular wave number (k) in terms of the wavelength (\lambda) of a wave.
angular-wave-number-definition-1c8a7d35.conceptual_definition: The angular wave number, often simply called wave number, quantifies the spatial frequency of a wave, representing the number of radians per unit length. It is directly related to the wavelength, which is the spatial period of the wave, or the distance over which the wave's shape repeats. This fundamental relationship connects the spatial oscillation characteristics of any wave phenomenon.
angular-wave-number-definition-1c8a7d35.interpretation: The angular wave number k indicates how many radians of phase change occur over a unit distance. A larger wave number implies a shorter wavelength, meaning the wave oscillates more rapidly in space. Conversely, a smaller wave number corresponds to a longer wavelength, indicating slower spatial oscillation. This concept is crucial in wave mechanics, optics, and quantum mechanics for describing wave propagation and interference phenomena, providing a measure of the spatial periodicity of a wave.
angular-wave-number-definition-1c8a7d35.limits_and_boundary: As $\lambda \to \infty$, $k \to 0$, meaning an infinitely long wave has no spatial oscillation. As $\lambda \to 0$, $k \to \infty$, implying an infinitely rapid spatial oscillation, which is physically unrealistic for continuous waves but can be approached in certain theoretical limits. Wavelength $\lambda$ must be a positive real number, as it represents a physical distance.
angular-wave-number-definition-1c8a7d35.symmetry_origin: This equation is a kinematic definition relating two fundamental properties of a wave (wavelength and spatial frequency). It does not directly arise from a specific symmetry or conservation law but is a consequence of how wave propagation is mathematically described in terms of spatial periodicity.

k.name: k
k.description: Angular wave number, representing the spatial frequency of the wave (radians per meter, rad/m).

inverse-of-time-d9812823.title: Reciprocal Time Scale (Frequency and Rate Parameter)
inverse-of-time-d9812823.description: Represents the algebraic inverse of a temporal duration or coordinate time, serving as the fundamental dimension of physical event rates, angular frequencies, and evolutionary expansion scales.
inverse-of-time-d9812823.conceptual_definition: The inverse time parameter $t^{-1}$ establishes the dimensional scale $[T^{-1}]$ for dynamic processes. In kinematic and statistical mechanics, it defines transition probabilities and event frequencies, while in cosmology and continuum dynamics, it parameterizes evolutionary rates such as the Hubble expansion rate $H(t) \sim t^{-1}$ or decay constants $\lambda = 1/\tau$.
inverse-of-time-d9812823.interpretation: The quantity $t^{-1}$ represents the rate of physical change with respect to time $t$. In dynamical systems, $t^{-1}$ characterizes the natural frequency $\omega$ or operational rate $k$. In cosmology, the reciprocal of cosmic time $t^{-1}$ approximates the Hubble parameter $H = \dot{a}/a$, defining the expansion rate of the metric spacetime.
inverse-of-time-d9812823.limits_and_boundary: As $t \to \infty$, the rate $t^{-1} \to 0$, corresponding to static equilibrium or asymptotic cosmic cooling. As $t \to 0$, $t^{-1} \to \infty$, representing high-frequency singular limits such as initial cosmological states or instantaneous impulse interactions.
inverse-of-time-d9812823.symmetry_origin: Dual to the continuous time-translation symmetry group $\mathbb{R}$, which by Noether's theorem gives rise to energy conservation $E = \hbar \omega \propto t^{-1}$ in quantum mechanics.

t.name: Time coordinate or characteristic duration
t.description: Temporal interval, characteristic timescale, or cosmic time coordinate

inverse-of-time-d9812823.intuitive_summary: Inverse time quantifies how rapidly events occur per unit duration, converting passive durations into active dynamical rates.

time-dependent-angular-position-6db14c19.title: Time-Dependent Angular Position Under Constant Angular Velocity
time-dependent-angular-position-6db14c19.description: Expresses the kinematic relation for the angular coordinate of an entity undergoing uniform planar rotation with constant angular velocity and vanishing initial angular displacement.
time-dependent-angular-position-6db14c19.conceptual_definition: The angular position $\theta(t)$ represents the accumulated rotational displacement in radians as a function of time $t$ for a system rotating at a uniform angular speed $\omega$. It arises from integrating the kinematic definition of constant angular velocity $\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t} = \omega$ subject to the initial condition $\theta(0) = 0$.
time-dependent-angular-position-6db14c19.interpretation: The equation models 1D rotational kinematics where $\theta(t)$ denotes the instantaneous angular position at time $t$, and $\omega$ denotes the constant rate of rotation. Multiplying the constant angular frequency $\omega$ by the elapsed duration $t$ yields the net angle traversed, assuming zero initial displacement $\theta(0) = 0$.
time-dependent-angular-position-6db14c19.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $t \to 0$, the angle satisfies $\theta(0) \to 0$. In the static limit $\omega \to 0$, the coordinate remains fixed at $\theta(t) = 0$. For unbounded $t \to \infty$, the cumulative unwrapped phase $\theta \to \infty$, whereas the mapped physical position coordinate wraps periodically via $\theta \pmod{2\pi}$.
time-dependent-angular-position-6db14c19.symmetry_origin: Continuous rotational symmetry $SO(2)$ in the motion plane and continuous time-translation symmetry $\mathbb{R}$, which by Noether's theorem relates to the conservation of orbital angular momentum $L_z$ and energy $E$ in autonomous central-force configurations.
